clue.text: Scottish dress (old-fashioned) one kept in sanctuary once

indicators.note: something kept in a place sits inside it, so one piece is held within the other

blocks.note: an obsolete word for sanctuary or asylum, hence 'once'
one as the indefinite article

explanation.surface: An old Highland costume preserved by someone who once took refuge in a church.
explanation.walkthrough: Grith is an Old English legal word for the protection of a church or king; 'once' marks it as obsolete.
explanation.definitionFit: Graith is an archaic Scots word for equipment or attire, so it covers the clothes a Scot once wore.

clue.text: Rat's scuttling in opening? This deals with foul smell (7, two words)

definitions.text: This deals with foul smell (7, two words)

indicators.note: rodents scuttling dart about every which way, so the letters are scrambled
the jumbled letters are placed inside the word for an opening

blocks.note: a gap is an opening
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A rat dashes into a hole, and someone wonders what will tackle the stench.
explanation.walkthrough: G(ASTR)AP. The rat and the smell suggest a drain, which is exactly where this device goes.
explanation.definitionFit: A gas trap is a U-bend in a drain whose standing water stops sewer gases rising into a building.

clue.text: Dance a Maori tripped around king

indicators.note: something tripped stumbles out of order, so the letters are rearranged
the jumbled letters go around the royal abbreviation, holding it inside

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
K is the chess abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: A New Zealander stumbles while dancing with a monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tripped' sounds like a dancer's stumble, and 'a Maori' suggests a haka, but the dance is Greek.
explanation.definitionFit: The romaika is a modern Greek folk dance performed in a ring.

clue.text: A parrot in song, note, referring to ancient deity

blocks.note: taken as written
Poll or Polly is the traditional name for a parrot
taken as written
an aria is a solo song in opera
N is the abbreviation for note

explanation.surface: A singing parrot hits a note in honour of an old god.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A parrot in song' reads as one bird singing, but every word supplies its own piece in turn.
explanation.definitionFit: Apollinarian means relating to Apollo, the Greek and Roman god of music and poetry.

clue.text: Measure in physics child on a lathe got wrong (9, two words)

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece placed on another sits above it, so it comes first
something got wrong is muddled up, so these letters are reordered

blocks.note: a tot is a small child
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A child in a school workshop makes a hash of a physics measurement on the lathe.
explanation.definitionFit: Total heat is the old term for enthalpy, a thermodynamic quantity measured in physics.

clue.text: Mangle leg twisted under hole in bog

indicators.note: something twisted is bent out of shape, so the letters are rearranged
in a down clue, a piece under another comes below it, so after it

blocks.note: in Scotland and northern England a hag is a broken, boggy hole in moorland
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A walker falls in a bog hole and badly twists a leg.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mangle' looks like the definition of something done to the leg, but it means to hack or cut roughly.
explanation.definitionFit: To haggle in its older sense is to hack or cut clumsily, so to mangle something.

clue.text: Some of the grub turned up as egg

indicators.note: only part of the following words is wanted, a run of letters inside them
in a down entry, turning something up means reading it from the bottom, so backwards

blocks.note: the last letter of the first word and the first three of the second

explanation.surface: Some of the food served up turns out to be an egg.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grub' and 'egg' both suggest food or insect larvae; egg is the verb, as in egg on.
explanation.definitionFit: To egg someone on is to urge them, so the verb egg is a synonym for urge.

clue.text: Evergreen causing hard grind for Aussie by the sound of it

indicators.note: the phrase tells us we want a word heard the same as the slang term, not spelt like it

blocks.note: Australian slang for hard work, spelt here as the plant name it is heard as

explanation.surface: An Australian complains that some tree is giving them a lot of hard graft.
explanation.walkthrough: Yakka is Australian slang for hard toil; the tree name is said the same way.
explanation.definitionFit: The yacca is an Australian grass tree, a plant that keeps its foliage all year round.

clue.text: Lined up as rolls of wadding, showing first bits only

indicators.note: only the opening letter of each word is displayed, the rest is discarded

blocks.note: the initial letters of the four words

explanation.surface: Rolls of padding are lined up so that only their ends are visible.
explanation.definitionFit: Arow is an old adverb meaning in a row, one after another, which is how lined-up things stand.

clue.text: Smart person with small bottle of Scotch – one may fashion dough in US

definitions.text: one may fashion dough in US

blocks.note: a smart cookie is a clever person
in Scotland a cutter is a small flask of whisky

explanation.surface: A clever operator with a hip flask of whisky ends up making money in America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dough' looks like money, but it is the pastry kind.
explanation.definitionFit: A cookie cutter is a shaped tool for stamping out biscuits, called cookies in the US, from rolled pastry.

clue.text: Conspiracy against getting involved in a bit of cash

indicators.note: to get involved in something is to be drawn inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: a coin is a single piece of money
V is short for versus, against

explanation.surface: A secret plot opposing someone ends up involving a little money.
explanation.definitionFit: Covin is an old legal term for a secret agreement between parties to defraud others, a conspiracy.

clue.text: Chaps putting away litre in content of tankard? Rarely pleasant

indicators.note: to put something away is to remove it, so that letter is taken out
the men are placed inside what is left of the drink

blocks.note: beer is what a tankard holds
L is the abbreviation for litre
chaps are men

explanation.surface: Blokes sinking pints of beer are seldom good company.
explanation.walkthrough: ALE loses its L, and MEN goes into the gap. 'Rarely' flags a rare word, not part of the meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: Amene is a rare literary adjective meaning agreeable, from French amène.

clue.text: Where directors convene to get on with reversal of dock?

indicators.note: the clue says outright that the word for dock is to be turned back to front

blocks.note: to get on a ship or train is to board it
to dock a boat is to moor it

explanation.surface: Company directors meet to sort out their differences with the harbour authority.
explanation.walkthrough: BOARD then MOOR read backwards as ROOM.
explanation.definitionFit: A boardroom is the meeting room where a company's board of directors gathers.

clue.text: Printer's odd-job man returned written work at fault

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came, so these letters are read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: MS is the abbreviation for manuscript
out as in wrong, mistaken, as in 'your sums are out'

explanation.surface: A print-shop handyman sends back a manuscript because it has errors.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the written work is turned round; 'at fault' follows unchanged.
explanation.definitionFit: A smout is printers' slang for a compositor who takes casual jobbing work rather than a regular post.

clue.text: Dance to jazz stuff – nothing found in music authority?

indicators.note: a thing found in a place lies inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: Grove's Dictionary of Music and Musicians is the standard reference work
nothing as the figure zero

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether jazz dancing would get a mention in the great music reference book.
explanation.walkthrough: GR(O)OVE. The definition takes in 'to jazz stuff', since the verb means moving to such music.
explanation.definitionFit: To groove is to dance or move rhythmically along to jazz or pop music.

clue.text: Get behind in changing late tax rate

indicators.note: something changing does not keep its form, so these letters take a new order
the word for falling behind is placed inside the other piece

blocks.note: to lag is to fall or get behind
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A taxpayer falls into arrears because a late change was made to the rate.
explanation.walkthrough: LAG goes inside TALE, a rearrangement of late.
explanation.definitionFit: Tallage was a medieval levy imposed by the Crown on towns and royal lands, so a form of taxation.

clue.text: Japanese 'untouchables' I'm getting muddled with bunraku

indicators.note: things getting muddled are jumbled up, so the letters take a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
the Japanese puppet theatre, taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: An outcast admits to getting confused about Japanese puppet theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: The burakumin are a Japanese social minority historically treated as outcasts, the country's equivalent of an untouchable caste.

clue.text: Bug heads for roughage in linen etceteras

indicators.note: heads are the leading parts, so only the opening letter of each following word is kept

blocks.note: the initial letters of the four words

explanation.surface: An insect turns up among scraps of fibre in the linen cupboard.
explanation.definitionFit: To bug someone is to annoy them, and to rile is to irritate or anger.

clue.text: Bubbly maybe after endless praise for poetic deluge

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter of the word for praise is dropped
the drink comes after, so it follows the other piece

blocks.note: to laud is to praise
champagne, bubbly, is one kind of this drink, hence 'maybe'

explanation.surface: Champagne flows freely after a round of tributes.
explanation.walkthrough: The word is borrowed from German Lawine, an avalanche, and survives mainly in poetry.
explanation.definitionFit: A lauwine is a literary word for an avalanche, a sudden overwhelming torrent of snow.

clue.text: Like a sourpuss dancing reel in the grass in America

indicators.note: letters that are dancing move about and land in a new order
the jumbled word is placed inside the American grass

blocks.note: in the US chess is a name for a weedy brome grass, also called cheat
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A grumpy figure is spotted dancing a reel on an American lawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reel' and 'dancing' make a dance scene, but the reel is only letters to jumble. CH(EERL)ESS.
explanation.definitionFit: A sourpuss is a habitually gloomy, sulky person, so cheerless describes their manner.

clue.text: West country chap in what sounds like merry frolics

indicators.note: the phrase tells us the answer is said like the word for the frolics, not spelt like it

blocks.note: lively bouts of fun, spelt as the dialect verb they are heard as

explanation.surface: A man from the West Country of England is caught up in merrymaking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chap' looks like a man, but it is the verb for skin cracking in the cold. The West Country is south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Spreaze is a Devon and Cornwall dialect verb meaning to roughen or crack the skin, as cold wind does.

clue.text: This woman chopped firs for Muslim rulers

indicators.note: trees that are chopped are cut into pieces, so these letters are reassembled differently

blocks.note: the pronoun for a woman
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A woman cuts down fir trees on behalf of the local emirs.
explanation.definitionFit: Sherif is a variant spelling of sharif, a title for descendants of the Prophet and for some Arab princes and governors.

clue.text: Vulgar goatish fellow sullied maiden

indicators.note: something sullied is spoiled from its original state, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the Greek god Pan had a goat's legs and horns
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A coarse satyr-like character has disgraced a young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vulgar goatish fellow' reads like one description, but only the first word defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Pandemian means common or popular, from Aphrodite Pandemos, the goddess of earthly as opposed to heavenly love.

clue.text: Tree yielding both oil and nuts? Draw up between two

definitions.text: Tree yielding both oil and nuts?

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from the bottom, so the word runs backwards
a piece placed between two others sits inside them, flanked on each side

blocks.note: to draw a cart is to pull it
two ones, each the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A gardener describes a tree producing oil and nuts, then sketches it between two others.
explanation.walkthrough: The reversed word goes between the two I's. The question mark is there because the oil comes from the nuts.
explanation.definitionFit: The illupi, or mahua, is an Indian tree whose seeds are pressed for an edible fat and lamp oil.

clue.text: Part of coastal defence, one to interrupt a swell, heaving (7, two words)

indicators.note: to interrupt is to break in, so this piece goes inside the other
something heaving is tossed about, so the letters are shaken into a new order

blocks.note: one as the indefinite article
taken as written

explanation.surface: A barrier on the shore is built to break up the heaving waves of the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: The extra A goes into 'a swell' and the seven letters are then rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A sea wall is a barrier built along a shore to stop the sea eroding or flooding the land.

clue.text: Ranged west in clan

indicators.note: the compass letter is placed inside the word for a family group

blocks.note: a sept is a branch of a clan, especially in Ireland or Scotland
W is the compass abbreviation for west

explanation.surface: The family moved about westward through the clan territory.
explanation.definitionFit: To sweep over an area is to range across it, so swept and ranged both describe moving over wide ground.

clue.text: Like a king or queen abandoned by prince beforehand

indicators.note: when someone abandons a word, that letter leaves it and is dropped

blocks.note: pearly kings and queens are London street traders in costumes covered with pearl buttons
P is the abbreviation for prince

explanation.surface: A royal is deserted by the prince ahead of time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'King or queen' points at royalty, but these are the costermonger kind. PEARLY loses its P.
explanation.definitionFit: Early means ahead of the expected time, so it serves as a synonym for beforehand.

clue.text: No longer last, race's leader coming in directly

indicators.note: the leader is the one at the front, so only the first letter is kept
a piece coming in enters the other word and sits inside it

blocks.note: due as in 'due north', straight or exactly
the opening letter of race

explanation.surface: A runner who was trailing comes straight through to lead the race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No longer last' looks like a runner moving up; here it means an obsolete verb meaning to last. DU(R)E.
explanation.definitionFit: Dure is an obsolete verb meaning to endure or continue, hence 'no longer' marking it as archaic.

clue.text: Wizard picture I dashed off

indicators.note: the letter dashes off and leaves the word, so it is dropped

blocks.note: an image is a picture
taken as written

explanation.surface: An artist quickly sketches a fantastic picture of a sorcerer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dashed off' suggests drawing a quick picture; here it means the I runs away.
explanation.definitionFit: A mage is a literary word for a magician or sorcerer, the same as a wizard.

clue.text: Mess left in small vessel

indicators.note: the single letter goes inside the word for a boat

blocks.note: a cutter is a small single-masted boat
L is the standard abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: Someone leaves an untidy heap aboard a little boat.
explanation.definitionFit: Clutter is an untidy jumble of things, an everyday synonym for a mess.

clue.text: Domiciled by Bohemia as was, wherein His Excellency resides

indicators.note: wherein means inside which, so the official's abbreviation sits within the other piece

blocks.note: CZ was the code for Czechoslovakia, the former state that contained Bohemia
HE is the abbreviation used for an ambassador's title

explanation.surface: An ambassador lives in a house in the old Czech lands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As was' tells us to use the former country, not today's Czech Republic.
explanation.definitionFit: Chez is French for 'at the home of', so it means living by or with someone.

clue.text: Account's settled in return of price paid – in this?

definitions.text: Account's settled in return of price paid – in this?

indicators.note: a return goes back the way it came, so the word for the fee is read backwards
something settled in has taken up residence inside, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: hire is the price paid for the use of something
AC is the usual abbreviation for account

explanation.surface: A debt gets cleared by paying back what was charged.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: an eriach is a payment in which an account is settled.
explanation.definitionFit: An eriach was the compensation fine paid to a victim's kin under old Irish law, settling the account for a killing.

clue.text: Evergreen timber, lustreless, of prime quality

blocks.note: matt or mat means without shine
A1, first-rate, written with the letter I standing for the figure 1

explanation.surface: A dull-finished but top-grade wood from a tree that never sheds its leaves.
explanation.walkthrough: A1 meaning first-class is often written AI in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: The matai is a New Zealand conifer whose hard wood is valued for building.

clue.text: Age with pulpit rumbling? It's filled in time of pestilence

definitions.text: It's filled in time of pestilence

indicators.note: rumbling suggests heaving and shaking, so the letters are disturbed into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: An old preacher's pulpit creaks while the church fills during an epidemic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Filled' sounds like a congregation filling the church; it is a mass grave being filled in.
explanation.definitionFit: A plague pit was a mass grave dug for victims of an epidemic and filled during the outbreak.

clue.text: Edmund's lost – he's following fringes of Tipperary

indicators.note: fringes are the edges, so only the outermost letters of the county name are kept
the man named comes after, so his piece goes second

blocks.note: the first and last letters of the Irish county
the 'he' is Edmund himself, and Ned is the pet form of Edmund

explanation.surface: Someone called Edmund has gone missing somewhere around Tipperary.
explanation.walkthrough: Edmund is Edmund Spenser, whose spelling this is; 'he' then points back to him, giving his short name Ned.
explanation.definitionFit: Tyned is Spenser's form of tined, past participle of tine, an old verb meaning to lose.

clue.text: Painter accompanying crumbling residence

indicators.note: the painter goes along with the following words, travelling inside them as a run of letters

blocks.note: the tail of the first word joined to the head of the second

explanation.surface: An artist goes with a friend to see a decaying old house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crumbling' looks like an anagram signal, but it is only part of the hiding place.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres was a French neoclassical artist famous for portraits and nudes.
